title: Causative and reciprocal
intro: [B1 unit 10](gp-passive) added two voices to the verb, the passive and the reflexive. This unit adds two more. The causative makes someone or something do the action: *Saçımı kestirdim* (I had my hair cut), *Beni güldürdün* (You made me laugh). The reciprocal is for what people do to each other: *tanıştık* (we met), *barıştılar* (they made up). The unit ends with the suffixes that turn nouns and adjectives into verbs: *temiz* → *temizlemek*, *güzel* → *güzelleşmek*.

blocks.text: A causative verb (*ettirgen çatı*) says that the subject makes or has someone else do the action, or makes something happen. Like the passive, its suffix comes right after the stem, and every tense and ending can follow: *yap-* (do) → *yaptır-* (have done, make do): *yaptırıyorum, yaptırdım, yaptıracağım*.

**You know some already.** Several verbs you have learned as words are causatives: *bitirmek* (to finish something) is the causative of *bitmek* (to end), *pişirmek* of *pişmek*, *geçirmek* (to spend time) of *geçmek*, *çıkarmak* (to take off) of *çıkmak*, and *anlatmak* (to tell, to explain) of *anlamak*.

blocks.label: The causative suffix (ettirgen çatı)
lines: -t     longer stems in a vowel, l, r:  oku-t, otur-t
-Ir    a few short verbs:              piş-ir, iç-ir

blocks.text: *-t* is for stems of two syllables or more that end in a vowel, l or r: *oku-t*, *bekle-t*, *otur-t*. Short stems take `-DIr`, even after a vowel: *ye-* → *yedir-* (to feed). The verbs with `-Ir`, `-Ar` and `-It` are a closed list, best learned as words.

head: Verb
Causative
Meaning
rows: to have (something) done; to make (someone) do

blocks.text: **Irregular.** Three common verbs have causatives of their own: *görmek* → *göstermek* (to show), *gelmek* → *getirmek* (to bring), *kalkmak* → *kaldırmak* (to lift, to raise; to remove). And *etmek* gives *ettirmek*, so every verb made with *etmek* has its causative in *ettirmek*: *tamir ettirmek* (to have repaired), *kontrol ettirmek* (to have checked).

rows.en: he or she had it done
you had it done (plural or polite)
he or she didn't have it done
Did he or she have it done?

blocks.caption: One causative, every tense: *yaptırmak* and *boyatmak* (to have painted)
head: Form
*yaptırmak*
*boyatmak*

blocks.text: A causative stem always has more than one syllable, so its aorist is `-Ir`: *yaptırır*, *okutur*, *gösterir*. After the *-t* suffix, the past and every suffix in `D` start with t: *boyattım*, *yıkattık*.

**Make, let or have done.** The same causative can mean **make** someone do something, **let** them do it, or **have** it done as a service: *Öğretmen bize çok ödev yaptırdı* (The teacher made us do a lot of homework), *Babam arabasını kimseye kullandırmaz* (My father doesn't let anyone drive his car), *Saçımı kestirdim* (I had my hair cut). Context decides.

items.en: I had my hair cut.
I had my car washed.
We had the house painted last summer.
I'm going to have my computer repaired.
Who cooked the meal?
Will you show me your photos?

blocks.text: *Saçımı kestim* means you cut it yourself. At the hairdresser's it is *Saçımı kestirdim*. Turkish uses the causative for any service: *Arabamı yıkattım*, *Evi boyattık*, *Ceketimi diktirdim* (I had my jacket made).

Some causatives have meanings of their own: *anlatmak* (to tell) from *anlamak*, *kaçırmak* (to miss a bus) from *kaçmak* (to run away), *uzatmak* (to make longer; to grow your hair) from *uzamak*, *kaldırmak* (to lift; to remove) from *kalkmak*.

sections.title: Saçımı berbere kestirdim: who does what

blocks.text: A causative adds a person or thing: the one made to do the action. Where it goes depends on the verb you start from.

**Verbs without an object.** The one made to act becomes the object, in the accusative: *Çocuk güldü* (The child laughed) → *Palyaço çocuğu güldürdü* (The clown made the child laugh). *Bebek uyudu* → *Bebeği uyuttum* (I put the baby to sleep). *Su kaynadı* → *Suyu kaynattım* (I boiled the water).

**Verbs with an object.** The object keeps its accusative, and the one made to act goes in the dative: *Ali raporu yazdı* → *Raporu Ali'ye yazdırdım* (I had Ali write the report). *Çocuk ilacı içti* → *Çocuğa ilacı içirdim* (I got the child to take the medicine). Leave the dative out and you describe a service: *Saçımı kestirdim*; put it in and you say who did it: *Saçımı yeni bir berbere kestirdim* (I had a new barber cut my hair).

blocks.caption: Accusative or dative
head: Plain verb
Causative
Meaning
rows: She put the baby to sleep.
She had Ali write the report.
He gave the child milk to drink.
She fed the baby the soup.

blocks.text: **Feelings.** Many verbs of feeling have a causative meaning **to make someone feel it**, with the person in the accusative: *sevinmek* → *sevindirmek* (to make glad), *kızmak* → *kızdırmak* (to make angry), *şaşırmak* → *şaşırtmak* (to surprise), *korkmak* → *korkutmak* (to frighten), *ağlamak* → *ağlatmak* (to make cry), *utanmak* → *utandırmak* (to embarrass): *Bu haber beni çok sevindirdi* (This news made me very happy).

**Let and not let.** With a negative, the causative often means **not let**: *Babam arabasını kimseye kullandırmaz* (My father doesn't let anyone drive his car). *Kullanmak* has an object, so *kimse* takes the dative.

items.en: The clown made the children laugh.
I've put the baby to sleep; be quiet now.
I had Ali write the report.
My mother fed the baby its soup.
This news made me very happy.
You kept me waiting for ages!

blocks.text: When the verb already has an object, the one made to act takes the dative, never a second accusative: *Ödevi Ali'ye yaptırdım*, not *Ödevi Ali'yi yaptırdım*.

French says faire + infinitive: J'ai fait couper mes cheveux, Il a fait rire les enfants. Turkish packs it into one verb: *Saçımı kestirdim*, *Çocukları güldürdü*. And the doer of a verb with an object goes where French puts it, with à: J'ai fait écrire le rapport à Ali is *Raporu Ali'ye yazdırdım*.

The reciprocal suffix `-(I)ş` (*işteş çatı*) marks an action two or more people do to each other: *görmek* (to see) → *görüşmek* (to see each other, to meet and talk), *tanımak* (to know) → *tanışmak* (to get to know each other, to meet), *bulmak* → *buluşmak* (to meet up). After a vowel it is just *-ş*: *tanı-ş-*, *anla-ş-*.

head: Verb
Reciprocal
Meaning
rows: to see each other; to meet and talk
to meet, to get to know each other

blocks.text: A few common reciprocal verbs have no plain verb in use beside them: *barışmak* (to make up, to make peace), *tartışmak* (to argue; to discuss).

**Who with whom.** With a plural subject, the verb says it all: *Dün tanıştık* (We met yesterday). With one person as the subject, the other comes with *ile*: *Annemle barıştım* (I made up with my mother). Both can also be the subject: *Ali ile Ayşe barıştı* (Ali and Ayşe made up; *barıştılar* is also correct). With a **we** ending, *X-le* often means **X and I**: *Ayşe'yle bir düğünde tanıştık* (Ayşe and I met at a wedding).

rows.en: he or she doesn't get along
Does he or she get along?

blocks.text: **Birbiri: each other.** Most verbs have no reciprocal form, so Turkish uses *birbiri* (each other) with a possessive ending for the people involved and the case the verb needs: *Birbirimizi seviyoruz* (We love each other), *Birbirinize yardım edin* (Help each other), *Birbirlerinden hoşlanıyorlar* (They like each other).
After a plural noun, the third-person singular forms are common too: *Çocuklar birbirine bakıyor* (The children are looking at each other).
**Together.** With some verbs, `-(I)ş` means doing something all together rather than to each other: *gülüşmek* (to laugh together), *koşuşmak* (to run around), *bağrışmak* (to shout all at once).

items.en: Ayşe and I met at a wedding.
Shall we meet tomorrow at five?
My brother and I get along very well.

items.tr: Çocuklar kavga etti ama hemen barıştılar.
items.seg: Çocuklar kavga etti ama hemen barış|tı|lar.
items.en: The children had a fight but made up right away.
We've known each other for years.
We used to write letters to each other.

blocks.text: Only some verbs have a reciprocal form, and its meaning is fixed by use. **We love each other** is *Birbirimizi seviyoruz*: the reciprocal *sevişmek* means **to make love**.

*Görüşmek* is everyday Turkish for **to see each other** or **to meet and talk**: *Görüşürüz* (See you), *Yarın görüşelim mi?* (Shall we meet tomorrow?). At work, a *görüşme* is a meeting or an interview.

sections.title: Temizlemek, güzelleşmek: verbs from nouns and adjectives

blocks.text: Many Turkish verbs are built from a noun or an adjective with one of four suffixes. Once you know them, you can guess verbs you have never seen and spot the family a word belongs to.

head: Suffix
What it makes
Examples
rows: to do something with the noun, or to make it so
to become (more) so; also to do together
*güzel* → *güzelleşmek* (to get nicer), *iyi* → *iyileşmek* (to get better), *zor* → *zorlaşmak* (to get harder), *mesaj* → *mesajlaşmak* (to text each other)
*ev* → *evlenmek* (to get married), *kir* → *kirlenmek* (to get dirty), *yaş* → *yaşlanmak* (to get old), *sinir* → *sinirlenmek* (to get annoyed)
*az* → *azalmak* (to decrease), *çok* → *çoğalmak* (to increase), *düz* → *düzelmek* (to improve, to get fixed), *kısa* → *kısalmak* (to get shorter)

blocks.text: The suffixes follow vowel harmony (*-la/-le*, *-laş/-leş*, *-lan/-len*, *-al/-el*), and the verbs they make are ordinary verbs, with every tense: *güzelleşiyor, güzelleşti, güzelleşmiş*. A k before `-Al` softens: *çok* → *çoğalmak*.
**A few `-lA` verbs also mean to become**: *zayıflamak* (to lose weight, [B1 unit 3](b1-u03)), *rahatlamak* (to relax, to feel relieved), *ucuzlamak* (to get cheaper), *yavaşlamak* (to slow down).

**Families of words.** `-lAş` is `-lA` plus the reciprocal *-ş*, and `-lAn` is `-lA` plus the *-n* of the passive and reflexive, which is why *mesajlaşmak* means **to message each other**. The `-Al` verbs make their causative with *-t*: *azalmak* → *azaltmak* (to reduce), *düzelmek* → *düzeltmek* (to correct, to fix), *kısalmak* → *kısaltmak* (to shorten).

items.en: This street has got really nice.
My mother was ill, but she's better now.
There are fewer trees in the city now.
My shoes got dirty.
I ironed my shirt.
Don't forget to water the flowers!
We texted each other all night.

blocks.text: French also makes verbs of change from adjectives: grand → grandir, vieux → vieillir, rouge → rougir. Turkish does it with `-lAş`, `-lAn` or `-Al`: *güzelleşmek*, *yaşlanmak*, *azalmak*.
Don't mix up `-lA`, which makes a verb, and `-lI`, which makes an adjective ([A2 unit 12](gp-li)): *tuzlamak* (to salt) but *tuzlu* (salty), *kirlenmek* (to get dirty) but *kirli* (dirty).

summary: The causative comes right after the stem: *-t* after a vowel, l or r in longer stems (*okut-*, *oturt-*), `-DIr` elsewhere (*yaptır-*, *güldür-*), `-Ir`, `-Ar` or `-It` on a few short verbs (*pişir-*, *çıkar-*, *korkut-*).
A causative can mean **make**, **let** or **have done**: *Bize ödev yaptırdı*, *Arabasını kullandırmaz*, *Saçımı kestirdim*.
From a verb without an object, the one made to act takes the accusative (*Çocuğu güldürdü*); from a verb with one, the dative (*Raporu Ali'ye yazdırdım*).
The reciprocal `-(I)ş` is for what people do to each other: *tanışmak, buluşmak, anlaşmak*; one subject takes the other person with *ile*: *Annemle barıştım*.
For other verbs, use *birbiri* with a possessive and a case: *birbirimizi, birbirinize, birbirleriyle*.
`-lA`, `-lAş`, `-lAn` and `-Al` make verbs from nouns and adjectives: *temizlemek, güzelleşmek, kirlenmek, azalmak*.
